title: Why people starve
hook: people starve because rulers take too much (Tao Te Ching 75)

segments.voice: Yesterday, threatening with death: a threat needs fear, and the hand that wields it gets cut. Your line was no threats. Did you swap one for a plain request? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

A cheap T-shirt in a shopping cart. A delivery that shows up in an hour. A price that seems too good. Somewhere behind each one is a person who carried part of the cost: the stitching, the late shift, the long drive. They don't appear on the receipt. Chapter seventy-five of the Tao Te Ching reads that kind of receipt for a whole country. It looks at hungry people and answers a question that is easy to skip: who took the bread?
screen: `A PRICE TOO GOOD.` → `NOT ON THE RECEIPT.` → `WHO TOOK THE BREAD?`

segments.voice: First, the hunger. The people are starving, the chapter says, because those above them eat up too much in taxes. That's why they starve. No talk of bad luck or lazy farmers. It points straight up the ladder. Second, the unrest. The people are hard to govern, it goes on, because those above them are always doing things, always busy with their own plans. That's why they're hard to govern. The trouble below is traced to the busyness above. Third, the recklessness. The people take death lightly, the chapter says, because those above chase after life too greedily. When the top grabs so hard at living, the bottom is left with so little that risking everything starts to look reasonable. Three problems, and each one is traced to the same place. Then the chapter closes on a quieter line: one who doesn't make a busy project out of living is wiser than one who prizes living too dearly. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. No crown is needed for this. Chains run through ordinary life too: a shopping cart, a payroll, a household, a group project. The chapter's habit is worth borrowing. When something goes wrong lower down, before asking what's wrong with them, ask what's being taken from above, and who carries it.
screen: `HUNGER: TOO MUCH TAKEN.` · `UNREST: TOO MUCH MEDDLING.` · `RECKLESSNESS: TOO MUCH GRABBING.` · `LOOK UP THE CHAIN.` · then, large: `WHO CARRIES IT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: consider who carries the cost. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Then bring to mind one ordinary thing from your day: a meal, a ride, something you bought, a task someone did for you. Follow it back one step. Who made it, moved it, cleaned up after it? Let one face or one role come to mind, even if you've never met them. Stay with that person for a while. You don't need to fix anything right now. Just let them be seen. The bell holds the time.
Why people starve. Chapter seventy-five: because those above take too much. Hunger, unrest and recklessness are all traced back up the chain. Today's word.
Your line: who carries it. Once today, before you blame someone below, look up the chain and ask who's carrying the cost. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-five as a sharp word to anyone in power: hunger, unrest and desperation below are traced to taking, meddling and grasping above.

pairs: those above take too much in taxes
the people are hard to govern

myth: chapter seventy-five blames hunger on the people's own laziness
it says the people starve because those above eat up too much in taxes.
the chapter traces three problems below to the same place above
hunger, unrest and recklessness are each traced to the rulers.
the chapter ends by praising those who prize life most dearly
it says one who doesn't make a busy project of living is wiser than one who prizes life too dearly.

fork.setup: you rule. your people are hungry and restless. where does chapter seventy-five tell you to look first?
options: at what those above are taking.
fork.reveal: the chapter points straight up: the people starve because those above take too much, and are hard to govern because those above keep meddling.

original.note: Chinese: the people's hunger, the opening of chapter seventy-five.

trapdoor: what you thought: why people starve is a question about famine.
what it means: the chapter traces hunger, unrest and recklessness below to taking, meddling and grasping above.
what a scholar hears: the same pattern, 'because those above...', runs three times, so the form itself teaches where to look.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 75 (the people starve because those above take too much in taxes; are hard to govern because those above meddle; take death lightly because those above seek life too greedily)

notes: Chapter 75 is paraphrased; the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording.
The third clause (以其求生之厚) is read here as 'those above chase after life too greedily'; some texts and translators read it as the people themselves seeking life too intensely. Confirm the reading.
The closing line (無以生為者，是賢於貴生) is paraphrased loosely; confirm.
The T-shirt, delivery and receipt examples are the writer's illustrations, not the text's.
Original 民之饑 (mín zhī jī) rendered 'MEEN jur JEE'. Confirm.
Editor: hook no longer says the chapter 'is about receipts' or 'asks' who took the bread; the chapter states the cause, so it now 'answers' that question.
